newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: FOCUS-Lithuania pushes privatisation in key areas.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lithuania pushes privatisation in key areas.

text.p: Lithuania's right-wing government on Wednesday took a step towards delivering key assets from state to private hands with the unveiling of a list of major companies to be sold through international tender in 1997-1998.
The government announced its intention to sell stakes in several key firms, including the telecoms company and a 49 percent stake in the state airline.
But analysts say the government must be ready to give up its majority stake in the companies if it wants to show it is serious about privatisation.
"This is what foreign investors would like to see, the big companies in these sectors sold off," Algis Avizienis, the head of the Lithuanian Investment Agency, told Reuters.
Prime Minister Gediminas Vagnorius came to power in November last year, ousting a government of former communists.
He has pledged to attract more foreign investment to Lithuania by selling key state firms that had previously been banned from sale as they were considered "strategic".
The government said it would keep at least 51 percent of the national airline and says it is not certain how much of a stake it plans to surrender in the telecoms compamy.
"This is an exciting development...Hopefully, the government will decide not to retain a majority," Avizienis added.
"It would be good if the government didn't just sell off percentages," he said.
Western analysts also said they were looking for the government to go one step further.

"If this government wants to put out a message that it is serious about attracting foreign investment, it must take radical steps and sell majority stakes in these companies," one Western analyst told Reuters.
Lithuania has been regarded as something of a laggard compared with Baltic neighbours Latvia and Estonia in the areas of privatisation and foreign investment.
Estonia has attracted most investment in the Baltic states, having been committed to a wide-ranging privatisation programme almost as soon as it quit the former Soviet Union in 1991.

Most small and medium-sized Lithuanian firms, shops, restaurants, farmland and residential housing were privatised in a first wave of selloffs but the state kept a grip on the transport and energy sectors.
Western analysts say these sectors are heavily subsidised, inefficient and in urgent need of reform.
The energy sector is caught in a vicious cycle of debt with consumers failing to pay even at subsidised prices and producers in turn failing to pay their suppliers.
